Alexa Prize 2018 dialog dataset (3,608 ten-turn movie dialogs)

changes_made.explanation: Consolidated dataset names to 'Amazon Alexa Prize Challenge (2018)', removed redundant/descriptive model names, and normalized BLEU spelling. The paper evaluates dialogue generation systems.

Removed baseline/model variants (BERT-Classification etc.) which are not standard metrics but experimental setups. Removed 'topical diversity' and 'conversational breadth' as they are mentioned in related work but not used for evaluation in this paper. Kept BLEU (as a baseline) and CMADE (the proposed metric).

Removed all metadata. The paper does NOT use an LLM as a judge. BERT is used as a feature encoder within the proposed model (CMADE), not as an external evaluator. The mentioned methods/criteria belong to human evaluation.

guideline: Experts annotated dialog pairs by answering: 'If you were the user, in which scenario would you be more likely to come back and talk to the system again?' Options were 'A is better than B', 'B is better than A', or 'cannot tell'.
- Experts are asked to choose which dialog in a pair would make them more likely to return, focusing on user experience.

Annotators were asked: "If you were the user, in which scenario would you be more likely to come back and talk to the system again?" They labeled 'A is better than B', 'B is better than A', or 'cannot tell'.
If you were the user, in which scenario would you be more likely to come back and talk to the system again?

changes_made.explanation: Consolidated the guideline into a single, clear description. Consolidated criteria by removing redundant entries ('User experience'/'user experience', 'Likelihood to return'/'likelihood to return') and removing 'Overall dialog quality' as it is not explicitly stated as a separate criterion.

overall_notes: The paper focuses on evaluating open-domain dialogue systems. The core contribution is CMADE, an automatic metric trained to predict pairwise human judgments of dialog quality. The human evaluation is carefully designed (pairwise comparison by experts) to create a reliable test set. The extracted metadata was generally good but contained some redundancy and items incorrectly placed under the LLM-as-judge question (Q3).
